# The Phantasia-Orexis-Kinesis Circuit: Nussbaum's Interpretation of Phantasia in Aristotle's Account of Animal Action 

## 1. Nussbaum on Phantasia (Imagination / φαντασία) The concept of φαντασία occupies a peculiar and perhaps deliberately ambiguous position within Aristotle's psychology of action, serving simultaneously as a residual motion derived from actual perception and as a functionally autonomous capacity that enables the animal soul to organize, interpret, and selectively present the perceptual world in a manner that renders it motivationally salient. Martha Nussbaum's influential reading draws our attention to the fact that phantasia is not merely a passive repository of after-images but rather an active, interpretive faculty that mediates between raw sensation and the arousal of desire; indeed, "phantasia and desire are jointly necessary conditions for animal motion," and furthermore that "phantasia is a necessary condition for desire," which must "'prepare' desire before" the animal can be moved to act (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 10). This preparatory function is critical: it establishes phantasia as logically and causally prior to orexis in the circuit of animal locomotion, and it distinguishes Nussbaum's reading from interpretations that treat phantasia as a mere epiphenomenon of perception. Aristotle himself distinguishes two grades of this faculty., "Sensitive imagination, as we have said, is found in all animals, deliberative imagination only in those that are calculative: for whether this or that shall be enacted is already a task requiring calculation; and there must be a single standard to measure by, for that is pursued which is greater" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). The distinction between sensitive and deliberative phantasia is thus grounded in the cognitive capacities of the animal in question; similarly, only creatures capable of calculation—that is, those possessing logos—can engage in the comparative weighing of future goods that deliberative phantasia enables (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). For animals that lack logos, sensitive phantasia alone provides the representational content through which objects appear as pleasant or threatening, and it is this appearing-as—this selective marking off and presentation of the perceptual field—that constitutes what Nussbaum terms "seeing-as." Phantasia is, accordingly, not to be confused with belief (doxa), since animals possess phantasia without possessing the propositional capacities that belief requires; nor is it identical with aisthesis, since phantasmata persist in the absence of the perceptual object and can be true or false in ways that mere sensation cannot (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 41–43). Indeed, Nussbaum notes that "after his attempt to distinguish phantasia from other cognitive faculties, Aristotle appends a discussion that explains delusion by false appearances, using a theory of motions (kinēseis) set up by actual perception, that remain even in the absence of the object and are 'similar' to the actual perceptions" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 41–43). The voluntariness of phantasia—whether the agent can summon phantasmata at will—remains a contested matter that we shall address more fully in a later chapter; for present purposes, it suffices Nussbaum emphasizes the active, selective character of the faculty, arguing that the "passive character of Aristotelian aisthesis" is precisely the reason "a further faculty is required agent's selective" engagement with the world (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 47). 

## 2. Nussbaum on Orexis (Desire / ὄρεξις) If phantasia supplies the motivating content—the "seeing-as" that presents an object under a desirable or aversive aspect—then orexis is the responsive movement of the soul toward or away from what has been so presented. Nussbaum's reading of the *De Anima* III.9–11 and *De Motu Animalium* 6–8 passages insists that desire is never self-originating in the absence of phantasia; thus desire does not arise in a vacuum but is always already prepared by the representational work of the imagination. As Nussbaum states, phantasia "is said to have two sources: sense-perception or thinking," and its being (the *einai*) "is different from the being of any other faculty, but that phantasia might still be 'the same as' some other faculty" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 22–24). This ambiguity notwithstanding, the functional role of phantasia in eliciting desire is clear: it provides the particular content under which the object of desire is grasped. Accordingly, the animal does not merely perceive water and then desire it; rather, the water appears to the animal as refreshing, as quenching, as the sort of thing toward which motion is appropriate—and it is this appearing, this phantastic presentation, that constitutes the proximate cause of orexis. Aristotle himself grounds this account in his analysis of the bodily mechanics of desire. In the *Movement of Animals*, "although from the point of view of the account which gives the cause of movement desire is the middle, and desire moves being moved, still in the animated body there must be some body of this kind" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, pp. 9–11). Hence desire occupies a mediating position: it is itself moved by phantasia and in turn moves the bodily apparatus that produces locomotion. The phrase "desire moves being moved" is particularly revealing, for it establishes desire as simultaneously active and passive—moved by the phantasmatic presentation and moving the animal's limbs. Nussbaum's reading exploits this double character the phantasia-orexis linkage is not merely a contingent psychological association but rather a necessary structural feature of Aristotle's explanation of animal action (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 10). Furthermore, Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotelian πάθος as "becoming-affected," or "being related to the world as in it, being in dealings with it," provides a complementary framework for understanding how desire constitutes a mode of being-affected by the world as it has been disclosed through phantasia (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 277–280). The animal is not a detached observer calculating utilities; it is, to some extent, always already immersed in a totality of involvements within which objects solicit desire through their phantasmatic presentation. 

## 3. Nussbaum on Kinesis (Movement / κίνησις) The culmination of the phantasia-orexis circuit is kinesis—actual bodily movement, the locomotive response through which the animal traverses its environment in pursuit of or flight from what phantasia has presented and desire has endorsed. Nussbaum's contribution here lies in demonstrating that the practical syllogism, as articulated in *De Motu Animalium*, compresses deliberative structure to the point where, in non-rational animals, it virtually disappears; what remains is the immediate transition from phantasmatic presentation through desire to locomotion. Thus to move a creature to action, an object must appear to it through selection, marking off, organization, and interpretation—processes that Nussbaum attributes to phantasia's "seeing-as" function—and the creature's desire must be engaged by that appearance (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 1–10; Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). The kinetic outcome is not incidental but structurally necessary: an animal that possesses both phantasia and orexis but lacks the bodily apparatus for locomotion would be, in Aristotle's framework, an anomaly requiring special explanation. Heidegger's reading of κίνησις as not merely physical displacement but a "how of being-there" enriches our understanding of what is at stake in this circuit. As Heidegger puts it, "movement is not a being, but a how of being-there, such that the how of this there is something already present: look" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 266). This kinesis is not an externally observable event separable from the animal's mode of disclosing its world; rather, movement is the very manner in which the animal's being-there is realized, and the "look" (εἶδος) that determines this movement is, in Nussbaum's terms, the phantasmatic content that has been prepared and presented to desire. Similarly, Heidegger's account of ἐνέργεια as a term that originated in the context of movement and was subsequently extended to other modes of actuality—"it happened that the name ἐνέργεια also came to be carried over to the other, to what contrasted with determinations of movement"—reinforces the primacy of kinesis in Aristotle's ontological vocabulary (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 213–215). Accordingly, the being-context of movement is determined by the category of πρός τι, the "being-in-relation-to-an-other," wherein the moving thing is characterized by ποίησις and the moved thing by πάθησις (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 232). In the case of animal action, phantasia and orexis together constitute the ποίησις—the productive aspect—while the bodily limbs constitute the πάθησις that receives and enacts the movement. 

## 4. Nussbaum and the Biosemiotic Dimension Nussbaum's interpretation of phantasia as "seeing-as"—as the selective, interpretive presentation of the perceptual world in a manner that motivates action—bears a striking, if historically unintended, resemblance to the biosemiotic framework developed by Jakob von Uexküll. In Uexküll's account, every organism inhabits its own Umwelt, a species-specific perceptual world constituted by the organism's particular sensory capacities and motor repertoires; within this Umwelt, objects do not appear as neutral entities but as carriers of significance, as Merkmalträger bearing perceptual marks (Merkzeichen) that are functionally coupled to the organism's action system. Uexküll himself insists that "every subject lives in a world in which there are only subjective realities and that even the Umwelten themselves represent only subjective realities" (von Uexküll, *Foray*, p. 69). This insistence on the subjectivity of perceptual worlds resonates with Nussbaum's emphasis on phantasia as an active, selective faculty that does not merely mirror external reality but constructs a motivationally structured field of appearance. Indeed, Nussbaum notes that Aristotle invokes a "theory of motions (kinēseis) set up by actual perception, that remain even in the absence of the object" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 41–43), and this residual motion—the phantasma—functions in a manner analogous to Uexküll's Merkbild, the perceptual image through which the organism recognizes and responds to features of its environment. What is perhaps most significant about this analogy is the shared emphasis on the organism's active role in constituting its experiential world: just as phantasia, for Nussbaum, is not passive reception but selective interpretation, so the Umwelt, for Uexküll, is not a pre-given environment but a semiotic construction shaped by the organism's biological endowments. However, we must exercise caution in pressing this analogy too far, for Aristotle's framework is fundamentally hylomorphic, grounded in the actualization of potentialities within a teleological order, whereas Uexküll's biosemiotics operates within a post-Kantian framework that foregrounds the constitutive role of subjective experience. 

## 5. Nussbaum and the Merkbild The specific concept of the Merkbild—the perceptual image or "mark-image" that mediates between organism and environment in Uexküll's biosemiotic theory—provides an illuminating point of comparison for Nussbaum's account of the phantasma. Uexküll describes how every animal's receptor system generates a perceptual field organized around biologically relevant features, and "the Umwelt concept has no room for the idea of a neutral, objective observation of things" (von Uexküll, *Foray*, p. 135). The Merkbild, in this account, is not a photograph of the external world but a selective, functionally organized representation that highlights precisely those features of the environment that are relevant to the organism's survival and action. Similarly, Nussbaum's phantasma—the product of phantasia—is not a neutral mental image but a motivationally laden representation that presents objects under the aspect of desirability or aversiveness, thereby "preparing" desire and initiating the kinetic response (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 22–24). The contested point, however, emerges when we consider the degree of cognitive sophistication required for this representational work. Nussbaum's reading, while attentive to the distinction between sensitive and deliberative phantasia, tends interpretive, quasi-cognitive character of even sensitive phantasia—the "seeing-as" that structures animal experience. Scholars such as Wedin have objected that Nussbaum's reading risks over-intellectualizing the faculty, attributing to animals a degree of representational complexity that Aristotle's text does not warrant. Furthermore, Nussbaum herself acknowledges the difficulty of specifying the exact nature of the causal connection between perception and phantasia; she concedes that Aristotle speaks of "calculation about the future as though it involved a kind of picturing" "the fact that noëmata are included here alongside phantasmata indicates that Aristotle is not committing himself" to a purely imagistic account of cognitive processing (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 53–55). The Merkbild analogy may thus illuminate the functional role of the phantasma without resolving the deeper question of its cognitive status. Indeed, the tension identified in the canonical concept nodes—between phantasia as causally derived kinesis and phantasia as functionally autonomous capacity—remains productively unresolved in Nussbaum's account, and it is precisely this tension that makes the biosemiotic analogy both illuminating and ultimately insufficient as a complete interpretive framework. Heidegger's characterization of perception as πάσχειν—as "becoming-affected" by "beings as world"—perhaps offers a deeper ontological register in which to situate this tension, for the animal's engagement with its environment is neither purely passive reception nor purely active construction but rather a primordial mode of being-in-the-world that precedes and grounds both (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 277–280). --- # VALIDATION APPENDIX ## Claim Map | # | Claim | Source | Page(s) |
